Introduction to Configuration Management
 Configuration Management (CM) is a systems engineering process that allows you to
configure your infrastructure and automate many tasks.
 Configuration Management (CM) is the process of systematically
 Managing
 Organizing
 Maintaining
 the configuration of computer systems, servers, applications, and network devices throughout
their lifecycle.
 It ensures that systems remain consistent, reliable, and secure by automating the
deployment, configuration, monitoring, and updating of infrastructure.
 In DevOps, Configuration Management plays a crucial role by eliminating manual
configuration errors and ensuring that all environments (development, testing, and
production) are configured identically.

-- 3 of 76 --

 Configuration Management is the practice of maintaining the desired
state of IT infrastructure using automation tools.
 It tracks changes, enforces standard configurations, and ensures that
systems remain compliant with organizational policies.
 In the last decade, a *plethora of configuration management tools hit the
software space.
 Tools like Ansible, Puppet, Salt, Chef, Terraform and many more offer a
wide range of capabilities to ease your infrastructure development.
 While they have many overlapping features, each software offers a
unique set of tools.
*Plethora - large amount of

-- 4 of 76 --

Before configuration management, system administrators configured
servers manually, leading to several problems:
 Configuration inconsistencies between servers
 Human errors during deployment
 Difficult troubleshooting
 Time-consuming setup process
 Poor scalability
 Security vulnerabilities due to misconfigurations
Configuration Management tools solve these problems through
automation.
Why is Configuration Management important?

-- 5 of 76 --

 In the era of microservices, we shouldn't configure each service manually: it's time-
consuming and prone to human error.
 Configuration management allows you to centralize and automate your
infrastructure configuration.
 An average web application has at least one database, a shared cache server, and a few
web app instances.
 When scaling horizontally, it's critical to be able to change configuration quickly and
revert in the case of disaster.
 To minimize user impact, the architecture should be resilient and immune to any outages.
 CM enables you to tame your infrastructure, reduce operation costs and cut downtime.

-- 2 of 108 --

Version Control Systems
A Version Control System (VCS) is a tool used in software
development and collaborative projects to track and manage
changes to source code.
 Tracks and records changes to the codebase, maintaining a
structured project history.
 Allows multiple developers to collaborate on the same project
without overwriting each other's work.
 Developers access and update a central repository, where project
files are stored.
 Enables teams to share updates and revert to earlier versions of the
project when needed.

-- 3 of 108 --

Component Explanation
Server
The central server stores all project files and their
complete version history. It acts as the main storage
location.
Repository
The repository is the central database that contains
the source code, documents, and all previous
versions of the project.
Developer 1,
Developer 2,
Developer 3
Multiple developers connect to the central
repository to download (checkout/update) files and
upload (commit) their changes.
Working of the Figure:
1. The Server hosts the central repository.
2. All developers connect to this repository through the network.
3. Developers download the latest project files from the repository.
4. They modify the files on their local computers.
5. After completing their work, they commit (check-in) the changes back
to the central repository.
6. Other developers can then update their local copies to receive the latest
changes.

-- 4 of 108 --

Components of Version Control Systems
Version Control Systems work using a few core concepts that help teams manage code changes
and collaborate efficiently.
 Repository: A central location that stores all project files along with their complete change
history and metadata like author and commit message.
 Revision: A specific saved version of a file or project, identified using a unique ID such as a
hash or number.
 Branch: A separate copy of the codebase used to develop features or fix bugs without
affecting the main code.
 Merging: The process of combining changes from one branch into another, which may
sometimes require resolving conflicts.
 Commit: A snapshot of changes made to the codebase at a specific time, used to track and
manage project history.

-- 5 of 108 --

Types of Version Control Systems
Local Version Control Systems (Local
VCS)
Centralized Version Control Systems
Distributed Version Control Systems

-- 6 of 108 --

Types of Version Control Systems
1. Local Version Control Systems (Local VCS)
A Local Version Control System (LVCS) stores all project versions on a single
computer and is mainly used by one user without remote collaboration.

What is DevOps?
 DevOps is a culture which promotes collaboration
between Development and Operations Team to deploy
code to production faster in an automated & repeatable
way.
 The word 'DevOps' is a combination of two words
'development' and 'operations.'

-- 4 of 55 --

DevOps Principles
 The main principles of DevOps are automation,
continuous delivery, and fast reaction to
feedback.
 DevOps pillars in the CAMS acronym:
 Culture represented by human communication,
technical processes, and tools
 Automation of processes
 Measurement of KPIs (Key Performance Indicators)
 Sharing feedback, best practices, and knowledge

-- 5 of 55 --

DevOps
 DevOps is a modern approach to software development that brings
development and operations teams together to deliver applications
faster and more reliably.
 It focuses on collaboration, automation, and continuous improvement
across the software lifecycle.
 DevOps is like a teamwork approach for making and delivering
computer programs.
 Encourages close collaboration between development and operations teams.
 Automates build, test, and deployment processes to reduce errors.
 Enables faster and more frequent software releases.
 Improves system reliability, monitoring, and feedback loops.

computing environment-from a developer's laptop to a massive cloud
production server.

DevOps Lifecycle
 The DevOps Lifecycle is a continuous, looping process that bridges the
gap between software development (Dev) and IT operations (Ops).
 Phases of DevOps Lifecycle
Phase 1: Plan (Dev)
Phase 2: Code (Dev)
Phase 3: Build (Dev)
Phase 4: Test (Dev)
Phase 5: Release (Ops)
Phase 6: Deploy (Ops)
Phase 7: Operate (Ops)
Phase 8: Monitor (Ops)
